approachQuestion.prompt:
Inventory summary

Return one (code, count) pair for each distinct integer code in a batch, with pairs in increasing code order. Count occurrences, including repeated codes. The input array may be reordered.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200,000; −1,000,000,000 ≤ code ≤ 1,000,000,000; codes are opaque comparison keys: radix, counting and bucket methods are excluded.

Examples: [8,2,8,2,8,5] → [(2,2),(5,1),(8,3)]. [7,7] → [(7,2)].

Choose the most efficient valid method among these options under the stated model; avoid removable repeated work.
constraints: The complete input/output and mutation contract in the prompt applies to every option.

options.text: Sort the codes, scan maximal runs of equal codes, and emit the value and length of each run.
options.feedback: Equal codes become contiguous, and run order already matches the required output order.

options.text: Scan the original order and emit a count whenever the code changes.
options.feedback: Equal values can be separated: [8,2,8] would produce two separate entries for code 8.

options.text: Sort the codes, remove duplicates, and emit count 1 for each remaining code.
options.feedback: Removing duplicates loses multiplicity: [7,7] needs count 2.

options.text: Repeatedly scan all unprocessed entries to find the smallest remaining code and count all of its occurrences, then mark those entries processed.
options.feedback: This produces the requested summary but can rescan almost the entire batch for each distinct code; sorting avoids that repeated work.

feedback.reason: Sorting makes equal labels contiguous, so a run count captures total frequency.
details: Comparison merge sort the input array, then scan equal-value runs with a scalar run length and append one pair per run.

Sorting makes equal labels contiguous, so a run count captures total frequency. Emit the final run too. Counting adjacent equal pairs would give frequency minus one rather than the required run length.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed method using conventional comparison merge sort with a linear merge buffer and a logarithmic recursion stack. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space bounds in n. Count all working copies, indexed records, buffers and stack frames; exclude the caller input and returned output. No hashing is used. Comparisons, arithmetic, record copies and array accesses take constant time; preallocate output capacity so no resizing assumption is needed.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) additional space
O(n log n) time, O(1) additional space

feedback.reason: Sort once and scan each equal-value run using a scalar count.
details: Sorting dominates the linear scan: O(n log n) worst-case time. The merge buffer use O(n) auxiliary memory; the O(log n) recursion stack does not change this total. The output is excluded. The quadratic-time option overstates the tight bound, constant space omits the buffer, and linear time omits comparison sorting.
